desc:
In a rectangular grid, 0 is a free cell and 1 is a blocked cell. A courier starts in the top-left cell and must reach the bottom-right cell. In one move the courier may go one cell right, one cell down, or one cell diagonally down and to the right, and may never stand on a blocked cell.

Return the number of different routes (two routes differ when their lists of visited cells differ), modulo 1,000,000,007. If the start or the destination is blocked the answer is 0.

grid = [[0,0],
        [0,0]]     ->  3     (right+down, down+right, diagonal)
grid = [[0,0,0],
        [0,1,0],
        [0,0,0]]   ->  4
constraints: The start and destination cells may be blocked
hints: This is the classic right/down counting problem with one extra kind of move. Think about which cells a route can come from when it enters a given cell.
A cell can be entered from above, from the left or from the upper-left diagonal. Let ways[r][c] be the number of routes ending there.
ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1] + ways[r-1][c-1] for a free cell, 0 for a blocked one, and ways[0][0] = 1 if the start is free. Take every sum modulo 1,000,000,007.
editorial: Every route into a free cell ends with exactly one of three moves, so the routes into it split into three disjoint groups: those arriving from the cell above, from the cell on the left, and from the upper-left diagonal neighbour. Hence ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1] + ways[r-1][c-1], where neighbours outside the grid contribute 0 and a blocked cell is set to 0 so no route can use it.

Fill the table row by row starting from ways[0][0] = 1. Each row needs the previous row, so a rolling pair of arrays gives O(n) memory; time is O(m · n). Without obstacles these numbers are the central Delannoy numbers on a square grid, which is a good way to sanity-check small cases (1, 3, 13, 63, ...).
